title: hatDu — Digital Request & Offer Platform
description: Designing a trusted digital platform where verified requesters and providers can connect, manage requests and offers, and collaborate through flexible account roles and permissions.
body:
# hatDu — Digital Request & Offer Platform

Designing a trusted digital platform where verified requesters and providers can connect, manage requests and offers, and collaborate through flexible account roles and permissions.

## The product

hatDu is a digital request-and-offer platform designed to connect people who need something with providers who can offer it.

The product brings together requests, offers, user accounts, verification, permissions and communication in one system.

As a Product Designer, I work across UX, UI, visual design and product communication — helping make a complex product easier to understand and use.

![hatDu request and offer platform interface](/images/home_Zeichenfl%C3%A4che%201%20Kopie%2018.jpg "hatDu — Post a Request and Receive Offers")

## My role

**Product Designer · UX/UI · Digital Experience**

I contribute to the product across interface design, user flows, responsive layouts, visual systems, product communication and design iteration.

I also work on supporting experiences such as product demonstrations, onboarding and educational content that help users understand how hatDu works.

## Timeline

**2022–2026**

## Context

### Designing for a product with real constraints

hatDu is not a simple interface or a single user flow. It is a working digital product with different user types, business requirements, verification rules and permission systems.

That means design decisions often have consequences beyond one screen.

A change to registration can affect verification.
A change to account roles can affect permissions.
A change to a request flow can affect both requesters and providers.

My focus is to make these relationships understandable through the interface without making the product feel unnecessarily complicated.

## The challenge

### How do you make a complex system feel simple?

One of the central design challenges was balancing flexibility with clarity.

The platform needs to support:

- **Trust** — users need to be verified before they can actively participate.
- **Different account types** — people can register privately or as a company.
- **Roles and permissions** — accounts can give controlled access to family members or colleagues.
- **Requests and offers** — the product needs to make two sides of an interaction understandable.
- **Real-world workflows** — users need to understand what happens before, during and after an action.

The goal was not to hide this complexity completely.

The goal was to **structure it so users can understand what they need to do next.**

## Product thinking

### Small UX decisions can change the whole product

Working inside a real product means looking beyond individual screens.

One example was the way users could work across different roles on the platform.

The original setup required separate login emails when a user needed to work in different roles. I proposed a simpler approach: allow one account to switch between requester and provider roles.

The idea was to reduce unnecessary account friction while keeping the distinction between the two roles clear.

### From account structure to user experience

The important question was not simply _“How should the screen look?”_

It was:

**“How should the product behave so the user understands where they are and what they can do?”**

This led to thinking about:

- how roles are represented
- how users switch between roles
- what actions are available in each role
- how the interface communicates the current context
- how the experience can remain understandable as the product grows

This is the kind of product-design problem I enjoy most: taking a complicated requirement and finding a clearer interaction model.

## A second example: Copy & Publish Request

Another product contribution was the **Copy & Publish Request** flow.

Instead of forcing users to recreate an existing request from scratch, the concept allows an existing request to be copied and its attributes edited before publishing again.

The underlying idea is simple:

**When users repeat an existing task, the product should help them reuse their previous work.**

This reduces unnecessary repetition and makes the workflow more efficient without adding another complicated process.

## Designing the product system

### Trust starts before the first request

Because hatDu connects people who need something with people who can provide it, trust is an important part of the product experience.

Users can register as a private person or as a company, but active participation requires identity verification.

Until verification is completed, users cannot post requests or make offers.

This creates an important product relationship:

**Verification is not just an administrative step — it is part of the user experience.**

The interface therefore needs to make the rules understandable without creating unnecessary friction.

### One account, controlled access

Another part of the product is account access.

An account can give controlled access to family members or colleagues instead of requiring every person to create and independently verify a completely separate account.

The super admin remains accountable for the account and can control what delegated users are allowed to do.

This introduces another layer of product complexity:

- Who is responsible for the account?
- Who currently has access?
- What can each person do?
- Which actions should require permission?
- How can the main account owner remain in control?

The design challenge is to make these relationships understandable while keeping the interface manageable.

### Designing for clarity, not just completeness

Systems like this can easily become complicated because every new permission, role or rule adds another layer.

My approach is to keep asking:

**What does the user need to understand at this moment?**

Instead of exposing every possible rule at once, the interface should provide the right information at the right point in the workflow.

## Interface design

### From structure to interface

Once the product logic is understood, the next challenge is translating it into interfaces that feel clear and consistent.

My work spans the relationship between:

- information hierarchy
- interaction patterns
- responsive layouts
- typography
- components
- visual consistency
- user flows

Rather than designing each screen in isolation, I think about how screens work together as part of the same product.

### Designing for different moments

A user may arrive at hatDu to:

- understand what the platform does
- register an account
- complete verification
- create a request
- browse existing requests
- make an offer
- manage account access
- work with information submitted by other users

Each of these moments has a different goal.

The interface needs to communicate the next useful action without overwhelming the user with everything the platform can do.

### Consistency creates confidence

For a product with many workflows and states, consistency becomes part of usability.

I work with repeated patterns across layouts, typography, buttons, forms, navigation and content hierarchy so that users can build familiarity as they move through the product. 

The goal is simple:

**The interface should feel like one product, even when the underlying workflows are complex.**

## Beyond the interface

### Design also has to communicate the product

A digital product is not experienced only through its interface.

For hatDu, I also create supporting visual and motion content that helps people understand how the platform works.

This includes:

- product demonstration videos
- animated explanations
- onboarding and educational material
- social media content
- visual communication for product features
- recorded website walkthroughs

### Making complex functionality easier to understand

When a product has multiple workflows and rules, a static screen is not always enough to explain the experience.

Motion allows me to show relationships between screens, demonstrate interactions and communicate a workflow more directly.

I use this as an extension of product design rather than treating motion as a separate discipline.

The same principle applies to educational content:

**If a feature is difficult to explain, the communication around the product should make it easier to understand.**

### A broader design role

Working across product, interface, motion and communication has given me a broader perspective on digital experiences.

I don't only think about how a screen looks.

I also think about:

**How will someone understand this?**
**How will they use it?**
**How will we explain it?**
**And how does it fit into the larger product?**

title: Gemeinsam Unterwegs — Digital Mobility Product
description: A route-based carpooling product concept connecting drivers and passengers through GPS-aware journey matching. I designed and developed the UX/UI, interactive journey form, mapping, matching logic, administration tools, data management and Excel reporting.
role: Product Designer · UX/UI · Web App · Mapping · Data
body:
# Gemeinsam Unterwegs

A digital carpooling concept designed to make everyday journeys more flexible by connecting people already travelling in similar directions.

## The problem

Public transport does not always match people's actual routes, schedules or daily needs. At the same time, many private cars travel the same roads with empty seats.

The concept explores a simple question: **Instead of creating another journey, can an existing journey be shared?**

## The concept

Drivers can offer available seats on journeys they are already making and receive a contribution towards travel costs. Passengers can find practical alternatives to waiting, walking or complicated public-transport connections.

## User experience

I designed the journey-entry experience around collecting enough structured information for meaningful matching while keeping the process understandable. The form captures role, start and destination, via points, dates, times, frequency, days, available seats, child-seat information, preferences, cost contribution and privacy confirmation.

## Interactive route mapping

The product uses Leaflet, Leaflet Routing Machine, OpenStreetMap/Nominatim and OSRM to turn Start → Via → Destination input into visual routes and structured geographic data.

## GPS-based matching

The matching concept considers route overlap alongside direction, travel days, travel times, available seats and journey characteristics. The goal is to identify practical compatibility rather than simply matching people who selected the same area.

## Administration & data

I developed an administration area for reviewing submitted journeys, including permanent journey IDs, journey details, route information, matching information and GPS data. Structured Excel reporting turns submissions into data that can be analysed and presented to organisations or potential partners.

## Product iteration

Testing with real journey submissions revealed an important product-design lesson: high GPS overlap alone does not necessarily mean two journeys are practically compatible. Different destinations, departure times and pickup requirements can still make a match unsuitable. This led to a broader matching model combining **route overlap + direction + time + day + pickup/drop-off compatibility**.

## Technical implementation

The prototype combines responsive HTML/CSS/JavaScript interfaces, interactive mapping, a custom WordPress-based solution, structured journey data, matching logic, administration, permanent IDs and Excel export.

## AI-assisted development

I used AI as a development accelerator while defining the product behaviour, UX, requirements and system logic myself. The project became an iterative cycle of **idea → user problem → UX → prototype → real submissions → data → matching → testing → refinement**.

## What the project demonstrates

**UX/UI Design · Interaction Design · Mapping · Data Design · Matching Logic · Administration · Reporting · Product Thinking · AI-assisted development**
